questions.q: "npm" is two things with one name. Which two?
questions.explain: The registry is the huge public library. The npm command, installed with Node.js, downloads packages from it, runs your scripts and publishes your own packages.
options: The public registry of packages at npmjs.com, and the npm command that installs from it
A programming language, and the program that runs it
The node_modules folder, and the package.json file
A code editor, and its plugin store

questions.q: Before you install a package you have not used before, what does the lesson tell you to do first?
questions.explain: Anyone can publish to the registry, so look before you install. npm view shows what the registry knows, including how many dependencies the package pulls in.
options: Run npm view <name> and check its description, source link, dependencies and licence
Install it with --force, so any problem shows up quickly
Install it globally, so it cannot touch your project
Nothing: every package on npmjs.com is checked by npm staff

questions.q: After npm install ms in a new project, which three things changed?
questions.explain: The code goes into node_modules, the range goes into package.json ("ms": "^2.1.3"), and the exact version goes into the lockfile.
options: node_modules/ms holds the code, package.json gains "dependencies", and package-lock.json appears
A copy of ms is added to your .js files, and package.json is deleted
Only node_modules/ms appears; package.json never changes
A .gitignore is created, and node_modules is committed

questions.q: The ms package is installed. What does this print?
questions.explain: ms turns text into milliseconds (2 days is 172,800,000 ms) and a number back into short text, or long text with { long: true }.
options:
2 days
10s
1h 1 hour

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ms rounds when it turns a number into text, so 90,000 ms (1.5 minutes) becomes 2m. Text it does not understand gives undefined. The README tells you about details like these.
questions.code:
import ms from "ms";

console.log(ms(90_000), ms(1_500), ms("hello"));
options: 2m 2s undefined
1.5m 1.5s undefined
2m 2s NaN
1m 1s 0

questions.q: You write import ms from "ms" (no ./ in front). Where does Node.js look for it?
questions.explain: A name without ./ or ../ is a package name, and Node.js looks for it in node_modules. It never downloads anything while your program runs.
options: In the node_modules folder
In a file called ms.js next to your script
On the npm registry, downloading it at run time
In the Node.js installation folder only

questions.q: Should you commit node_modules to Git?
questions.explain: node_modules can hold thousands of files and is rebuilt with one command. The lockfile, on the other hand, must be committed.
options: No: put it in .gitignore; anyone can rebuild it from package.json and the lockfile
Yes, so the server does not need to install anything
Yes, but only the packages from devDependencies
No, and you should not commit package-lock.json either

questions.q: Which package belongs in devDependencies (npm install -D)?
questions.explain: Dev dependencies are tools for developing: formatters, test runners, TypeScript. Anything your program imports while it runs is a normal dependency.
options: Prettier, a code formatter you only run while writing code
ms, which your server calls to compute due dates
The database driver your API uses to save tasks
A ZudoJS package that your server imports

questions.q: Why does it help to keep tools like Prettier out of the normal dependencies?
questions.explain: Every installed package is code from strangers. Leaving tools off the server means less code there that could be attacked.
options: A production server installs only normal dependencies, so it is smaller and has less code for attackers to aim at
Dev dependencies are downloaded faster
Normal dependencies cannot contain command-line tools
It makes the tools run without Node.js

questions.q: What does "type": "module" in package.json do?
questions.explain: With "type": "module", Node.js treats your .js files as ES modules. You set it with npm pkg set type=module.
options: It makes .js files ES modules, so they use import and export
It publishes the project as a package
It marks every dependency as a dev dependency
It tells npm to install TypeScript

questions.q: package.json is plain JSON, so code can read it. What does this print?
questions.explain: The file has no peerDependencies, so pkg[section] is undefined, and ?? {} gives an empty object with 0 keys instead of throwing.
options:
task-tools 1.0.0
dependencies 1
devDependencies 2
peerDependencies 0

task-tools 1.0.0
dependencies 1
devDependencies 2

task-tools 1.0.0
dependencies 1
devDependencies 2
peerDependencies undefined

task-tools ^1.0.0
dependencies 1
devDependencies 2
peerDependencies 0

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: start and test are special names that work without run. Every other script needs npm run <name>.
options:
npm start -> node due.js
npm run format -> prettier --write .
npm run check-format -> prettier --check .

npm run start -> node due.js
npm run format -> prettier --write .
npm run check-format -> prettier --check .

npm start -> node due.js
npm format -> prettier --write .
npm check-format -> prettier --check .

questions.q: The script "format": "prettier --write ." works even though prettier is not installed globally. Why?
questions.explain: When npm runs a script, the tools from node_modules are available by name, so you don't need npx or a global install.
options: npm scripts can call tools installed in the project's node_modules directly
npm downloads Prettier again every time the script runs
Prettier is built into Node.js
The . at the end tells npm where Prettier is

questions.q: npm run check-format finds a badly formatted file. Why is it useful that it ends with a non-zero exit code?
questions.explain: Exit code 0 means success, anything else means failure. Automated builds look at the exit code, not at the text, to decide whether a step passed.
options: An automated check can see the failure and stop, for example before code is merged
It makes the terminal print the file in red
It deletes the badly formatted file
It is not useful; it is a bug in Prettier

questions.q: What does the script "dev": "node --watch server.js" do?
questions.explain: --watch is built into Node.js. It is handy while writing a server: save, and the new code is already running.
options: It runs server.js and restarts it every time you save a file
It watches the npm registry for new versions of your packages
It runs server.js in the background after you close the terminal
It checks server.js for security problems

questions.q: A package goes from 2.1.3 to 3.0.0. What does semantic versioning tell you?
questions.explain: In MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, PATCH is for bug fixes, MINOR for new features that keep old code working, and MAJOR for changes that can break it.
options: Something changed in a way that can break your code: read the changelog before upgrading
Only bugs were fixed
New features were added, and nothing can break
Nothing: the numbers are chosen at random

questions.q: Your package.json says "ms": "^2.1.0". Which version could npm install?
questions.explain: A caret accepts new minor and patch versions, starting at the version given, but never a new major. So 2.9.0 fits; 2.0.0 is too old and 3.0.0 is a new major.
options: 2.9.0
2.0.0
3.0.0
1.9.9

questions.q: Your package.json says "ms": "~2.0.1". Which versions from this list could npm install: 2.0.0, 2.0.1, 2.0.9, 2.1.0, 3.0.0?
questions.explain: A tilde range allows only newer patch versions, starting at the version given. 2.1.0 is a new minor, and 2.0.0 is older than 2.0.1.
options: 2.0.1 and 2.0.9
2.0.1, 2.0.9 and 2.1.0
Only 2.0.1
2.0.0, 2.0.1 and 2.0.9

questions.q: What does a range with no symbol, like "ms": "2.1.0", accept?
questions.explain: No symbol means exact: that version and nothing else. npm install writes a caret (^) by default.
options: Only version 2.1.0
Any 2.x version
Any 2.1.x version
The latest version, whatever it is

questions.q: Why does ^0.2.0 accept only 0.2.x versions, and not 0.3.0?
questions.explain: Versions starting with 0. are treated as unstable. Edge cases like this are why real code uses the semver package instead of a hand-written check.
options: Before 1.0.0, every minor version may break things, so the caret is stricter
Because a version cannot start with 0
Because npm never installs versions below 1.0.0
It is a bug in npm; 0.3.0 should be accepted

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: map(Number) turns each part into a number. Comparing whole version strings is wrong: text is compared character by character, and "1" comes before "9", so "2.10.0" > "2.9.0" is false.

questions.q: This is the lesson's caret check. What does it print?
questions.explain: The major number must be 1, and the version must be at least 1.4.0. 1.3.9 is too old, 1.10.0 is newer (10 is more than 4 as a number), and 2.0.0 is a new major.
options: [ true, false, true, false ]
[ true, false, false, false ]
[ true, true, true, false ]
[ true, false, true, true ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Plain sort() compares text, so 2.10.0 lands before 2.9.0. Comparing the numbers part by part gives the real order.

questions.q: You type npx semvr --range "^2.1.0" 2.9.0 (with a typo) and npx asks "Ok to proceed?". What should you do?
questions.explain: npx downloads a package and runs it on your computer. A spelling mistake can run someone else's package, so read the name before you type y.
options: Answer no: npx would download and run an unknown package with your permissions
Answer yes: npx only runs packages that npm has checked
Answer yes: npx runs packages in a safe sandbox
Answer yes, then delete node_modules afterwards

questions.q: What does package-lock.json record?
questions.explain: A range can match a different version next month. The lockfile pins the exact version, the download address and an integrity hash, so everyone gets the same code.
options: The exact version of every installed package, where it came from, and a hash of its contents
The ranges you typed, such as ^2.1.3, and nothing else
The passwords npm uses to log in to the registry
A list of packages that failed to install

questions.q: What does npm do with the integrity value in the lockfile?
questions.explain: integrity is a SHA-512 fingerprint of the package. If the file you download has been changed, the fingerprint differs and npm stops.
options: It hashes the downloaded package and refuses to install it if the hash does not match
It uses it as a password to download private packages
It sends it to the author to count downloads
It decrypts the package with it

questions.q: Which command should a server or an automated build use to install packages?
questions.explain: npm ci ("clean install") gives the server the code you tested, byte for byte. If package.json and the lockfile are out of sync, it stops instead of guessing.
options: npm ci, which installs exactly what the lockfile says and fails if it disagrees with package.json
npm install, which may quietly move to newer versions in your ranges
npm update, so the server always has the newest versions
npm install --force, so it never fails

questions.q: npm outdated shows ms Current 2.0.0 Wanted 2.1.3 Latest 3.0.0. What does "Wanted" mean?
questions.explain: Current is what is installed, Wanted is the newest version your range allows, and Latest is the newest version published. npm update moves to Wanted.
options: The newest version your range in package.json allows
The newest version ever published
The version your team voted for
The version that is installed now

questions.q: ms is at 2.1.3, the range is ^2.0.0, and 3.0.0 is out. What happens when you run npm update?
questions.explain: A major version can break your code, so you move to it on purpose with npm install ms@latest, after reading the changelog.
options: Nothing for ms: npm update never crosses a major version
ms moves to 3.0.0
npm asks whether you want 3.0.0
ms is removed, because it is out of date

questions.q: This works out what npm outdated calls "Wanted". What does it print?
questions.explain: With a caret range on major 2, the newest allowed version is 2.4.1. "Latest" ignores your range and is simply the newest published version.
options: Wanted: 2.4.1 Latest: 3.1.0
Wanted: 3.1.0 Latest: 3.1.0
Wanted: 2.0.0 Latest: 3.1.0
Wanted: 2.4.1 Latest: 2.4.1

questions.q: What do npm workspaces let you do?
questions.explain: The root lists package folders with "workspaces": ["packages/*"]. npm install links them into node_modules, so a change in the folder is seen at once.
options: Keep several local packages in one project and import them by name, without publishing them
Install packages for several users on one computer
Run several scripts at the same time
Publish a package under several names

questions.q: Why does the workspace root's package.json have "private": true?
questions.explain: npm refuses to publish a package marked private. The root only groups the real packages, so it should never be published.
options: It stops the root from ever being published by accident
It hides the code from other developers on the team
It encrypts the packages folder
It makes every package in the workspace private on npmjs.com

questions.q: What should you always do before npm publish?
questions.explain: The registry is public and permanent. npm pack --dry-run lists the files without sending anything, so you can spot a test file or, much worse, a .env.
options: Run npm pack --dry-run and read exactly which files would be uploaded
Delete package.json, which npm does not need
Run npm audit fix --force
Publish once to test, then unpublish

questions.q: A package folder contains index.js, index.test.js and a .env file with secrets. What is the safe way to publish only index.js?
questions.explain: By default npm packs everything in the folder, including .env. An allow-list keeps every new file private until you add it on purpose. A secret that was published once must be treated as leaked.
options: Add "files": ["index.js"] to package.json, an allow-list, and check with npm pack --dry-run
Nothing: npm never publishes .env files
Rename .env to .env.secret
Publish, then delete the .env file in a new version

questions.q: What does npm audit do?
questions.explain: npm audit reports packages with known vulnerabilities, how serious they are and whether a fixed version exists. npm audit fix moves to a fixed version inside your range.
options: It compares your installed versions with a public list of known security problems
It reads every package's code and finds new bugs
It checks that your code is formatted
It deletes packages nobody has updated in a year

questions.q: npm audit suggests npm audit fix --force. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Plain npm audit fix stays inside your ranges. --force is allowed to cross a major version, so check the changes before you use it.
options: --force may jump to a new major version, which can break your code; read what it will change first
It uninstalls every package with a problem
It turns off security checks for the future
There is no risk; it is the same as npm audit fix

questions.q: A package you have never heard of asks to run an install script. What should you do?
questions.explain: An install script can do anything your user can do, which is why malicious packages love them. Only approve a script you have reviewed from a package you trust.
options: Deny it with npm install-scripts deny and find out why it is in your project with npm ls
Approve it, because install scripts only download files
Approve it, then run npm audit to see if it did anything bad
Delete package-lock.json and install again

questions.q: After npm install-scripts approve esbuild, package.json contains "allowScripts": { "esbuild@0.28.2": true }. What happens when esbuild releases a new version?
questions.explain: The approval is pinned to one version. A new version could contain a changed script, so you review it again.
options: npm asks you again, because the approval is for the version you reviewed
The new version's script runs automatically, because esbuild is approved
npm removes esbuild from your project
The script never runs again

questions.q: What is typosquatting?
questions.explain: In 2017, crossenv copied the popular cross-env and sent everyone's environment variables to its author. Copy names from official docs and check them with npm view.
options: Publishing a package whose name is one typo away from a popular one, hoping people mistype it
Writing code with many spelling mistakes
Taking over a package whose author forgot to renew it
Using a package name in capital letters

questions.q: What does provenance on an npm package tell you?
questions.explain: Provenance lets you trace a package back to its source. npm audit signatures checks it, and you add --provenance to npm publish when publishing from GitHub Actions.
options: A signed statement of which source repository and which automated build produced the package
That npm staff reviewed the code for bugs
That the package has no known vulnerabilities
How many people downloaded the package this week

questions.q: Finish satisfiesTilde(version, range) for plain MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbers. A tilde range like ~2.0.1 accepts versions with the same major and minor numbers and a patch number at least as big.
questions.explain: Remove the ~, split both versions and turn the parts into numbers. Major and minor must be equal, and the patch must be at least the base patch. Comparing numbers (not text) makes 2.0.10 pass.

questions.q: Finish bump(version, part), like npm version patch|minor|major. Raising a part sets the parts after it to 0.
questions.explain: Split the version into three numbers. A major bump resets minor and patch, a minor bump resets patch, and a patch bump only adds 1 to the last number (so 0.9.9 becomes 0.9.10).

questions.q: Finish describeRange(range). Return "new minor and patch" for a caret range, "new patch only" for a tilde range, and "exact" for a range with no symbol.
questions.explain: Look at the first character: ^ accepts new minor and patch versions, ~ only new patches, and no symbol means that exact version.
questions.expected:
^2.1.3 -> new minor and patch
~2.1.3 -> new patch only
2.1.3 -> exact

questions.q: Finish newest(versions), which returns the highest version in the list. Compare the numbers part by part; comparing whole strings is wrong ("2.10.0" < "2.9.0" as text).
questions.explain: Turn each version into three numbers and compare major first, then minor, then patch. a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1] || a[2] - b[2] is positive when a is newer.

questions.q: Finish listDeps(pkg). Return one line per package, section: name range, for dependencies first and then devDependencies. A missing section must not throw.
questions.explain: Loop over the two section names, and use Object.entries(pkg[section] ?? {}) so a missing section counts as empty instead of throwing.

questions.q: Finish filesToPublish(folderFiles, allow), like npm's files allow-list. Keep only the files named in allow, plus package.json and README.md, which npm always adds. Keep the order of folderFiles.
questions.explain: An allow-list starts from "nothing" and adds what you name, so .env, tests and notes stay out automatically. filter keeps the original order.

questions.q: This copies the check npm ci makes before installing. What does it print?
questions.explain: 2.1.3 fits ^2.0.0 (same major). Someone then changed package.json to the exact 1.0.0 without running npm install, so the lockfile no longer fits and npm ci refuses to continue.
options:
in sync
lock file's ms@2.1.3 does not satisfy ms@1.0.0

in sync
in sync

lock file's ms@2.1.3 does not satisfy ms@^2.0.0
lock file's ms@2.1.3 does not satisfy ms@1.0.0

in sync
lock file's ms@1.0.0 does not satisfy ms@2.1.3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1.5 hours is 5,400,000 ms, which is 90 minutes. Turning it back into short text rounds to the nearest hour, 2h: a detail the README warns you about.
